1b:["$","$L6","1",{"href":"/areas/civil-rights","className":"text-[9px] uppercase tracking-tighter bg-sand px-2 py-1 border border-gold/20 hover:border-gold transition-colors","children":"Civil Rights"}]
1c:["$","div",null,{"className":"lg:col-span-8","children":[["$","header",null,{"className":"mb-12","children":[["$","h1",null,{"className":"font-serif font-light text-5xl md:text-6xl text-navy mb-4 leading-tight","children":"Queen Agnes"}],["$","div",null,{"className":"w-24 h-[2px] bg-gold"}]]}],["$","section",null,{"className":"prose prose-navy max-w-none","children":[["$","div",null,{"className":"relative mb-12","children":[["$","$L1a",null,{"ref":"$undefined","iconNode":[["path",{"d":"M16 3a2 2 0 0 0-2 2v6a2 2 0 0 0 2 2 1 1 0 0 1 1 1v1a2 2 0 0 1-2 2 1 1 0 0 0-1 1v2a1 1 0 0 0 1 1 6 6 0 0 0 6-6V5a2 2 0 0 0-2-2z","key":"rib7q0"}],["path",{"d":"M5 3a2 2 0 0 0-2 2v6a2 2 0 0 0 2 2 1 1 0 0 1 1 1v1a2 2 0 0 1-2 2 1 1 0 0 0-1 1v2a1 1 0 0 0 1 1 6 6 0 0 0 6-6V5a2 2 0 0 0-2-2z","key":"1ymkrd"}]],"className":"lucide-quote absolute -left-8 -top-8 h-16 w-16 text-gold/10 pointer-events-none"}],["$","h2",null,{"className":"font-serif font-bold text-3xl text-navy mb-6","children":"Biography"}],["$","div",null,{"className":"text-navy/80 text-xl leading-relaxed prose prose-navy max-w-none  prose-headings:font-serif prose-headings:font-bold prose-headings:text-navy  prose-h3:text-3xl prose-h3:mt-10 prose-h3:mb-4 prose-a:text-gold hover:prose-a:text-navy prose-a:transition-colors prose-img:rounded-md prose-img:shadow-md prose-img:mx-auto prose-img:border prose-img:border-gold/20 prose-blockquote:border-l-4 prose-blockquote:border-gold prose-blockquote:pl-8  prose-blockquote:italic prose-blockquote:text-navy/80 prose-blockquote:font-serif prose-blockquote:text-2xl prose-blockquote:ml-8 prose-blockquote:my-10 [&_blockquote_p::before]:hidden [&_blockquote_p::after]:hidden","children":[["$","h3","h3-0",{"children":"Introduction"}],"\n",["$","p","p-0",{"children":["Axeline \"Queen Agnes\" Elizabeth Salomon (c. 1858 – after 1888) was a legendary labor leader and resistance fighter in the Danish West Indies (modern-day U.S. Virgin Islands). She rose to historical prominence as one of the \"Four Queens\" who led the historic 1878 labor rebellion on the island of St. Croix, an event popularly known as the \"Fireburn\" [1]. Alongside ",["$","$L1d","a-0",{"slug":"queen-mary","href":"/profiles/queen-mary","children":"Queen Mary"}]," (Mary Thomas), ",["$","$L1d","a-1",{"slug":"queen-mathilda","href":"/profiles/queen-mathilda","children":"Queen Mathilda"}]," (Mathilda McBean), and Susana \"Bottom Belly\" Abramsen, Queen Agnes organized and mobilized plantation laborers to rise up against the oppressive, semi-feudal labor contracts imposed by Danish colonial authorities [2]. Her actions during the revolt, particularly at the Carlton Plantation, and her subsequent imprisonment in Denmark and St. Croix, made her a symbol of Caribbean working-class resistance, gendered leadership, and the struggle for human dignity."]}],"\n",["$","p","p-1",{"children":["$","img","img-0",{"src":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/4c/ThreeQueensSTT.jpg","alt":"The Three Queens Fountain monument in Charlotte Amalie, St. Thomas, featuring Queen Mary, Queen Agnes, and Queen Mathilda"}]}],"\n",["$","h3","h3-1",{"children":"Socio-Economic Context: Post-Emancipation Peonage"}],"\n",["$","p","p-2",{"children":"To understand the rise of Queen Agnes, one must examine the socio-economic conditions of St. Croix in the mid-to-late nineteenth century. In 1848, Governor Peter von Scholten officially emancipated the enslaved population of the Danish West Indies in the face of a massive, organized uprising of enslaved workers. However, the plantocracy and the Danish colonial government quickly moved to subvert this newly won freedom. In 1849, the colonial administration enacted the Labor Act (Arbejdsregulativet), which designed a system of debt peonage that bound formerly enslaved workers to their plantations in conditions that closely mirrored slavery [3]."}],"\n","$L1e","\n","$L1f","\n","$L20","\n","$L21","\n","$L22","\n","$L23","\n","$L24","\n","$L25","\n","$L26","\n","$L27","\n","$L28","\n","$L29","\n","$L2a","\n","$L2b","\n","$L2c","\n","$L2d","\n","$L2e","\n","$L2f","\n","$L30","\n","$L31","\n","$L32","\n","$L33","\n","$L34","\n","$L35","\n","$L36","\n","$L37","\n","$L38","\n","$L39","\n","$L3a","\n","$L3b","\n","$L3c","\n","$L3d","\n","$L3e"]}]]}],"$L3f","$L40",false]}],"$L41"]}]
42:I[54477,["/_next/static/chunks/2i9p3n79r-dbf.js","/_next/static/chunks/2z-jpqdx1wamk.js","/_next/static/chunks/14mrh2-p_w84d.js","/_next/static/chunks/2uyb8-0enc77-.js","/_next/static/chunks/2zpyn7ne_o0vv.js"],"default"]
:HL["https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/5a/Frederiksted%2C_St_Croix_U.S._Virgin_Islands.JPG","image"]
:HL["https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/df/John_R._Neill%2C_noted_illustrator.jpg/960px-John_R._Neill%2C_noted_illustrator.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=api&utm_content=thumbnail","image"]
1e:["$","p","p-3",{"children":"Under this act, laborers were forced to sign annual contracts. They were classified as \"first-class,\" \"second-class,\" or \"third-class\" workers, receiving extremely low wages. They were required to work long, grueling hours—typically from sunrise to sunset—and were forbidden from leaving their plantations without written permission from their employers. The only day of the year when workers were permitted to terminate their contracts, seek new employers, or leave their estates was October 1st, which became known as \"Contract Day\" or \"Quarter Day\" [3]."}]
1f:["$","p","p-4",{"children":"By 1878, thirty years after emancipation, the laborers’ frustration reached a boiling point. Wages had stagnated or decreased, inflation had driven up the cost of basic goods, and the island had suffered from droughts and crop failures. Laborers realized that despite their legal freedom, they were trapped in a cycle of poverty and exploitation with no upward mobility."}]
20:["$","h3","h3-2",{"children":"Early Life and Identity of Axeline Salomon"}]
21:["$","p","p-5",{"children":"Axeline Elizabeth Salomon, who was commonly known by her middle name, Agnes, was born on St. Croix around 1858. Unlike the wealthy colonial administrators who kept detailed journals, the lives of Black working-class women like Agnes were rarely recorded in detail unless they ran afoul of the colonial legal system. Consequently, much of what historians know about Agnes’s early life comes from the police records, census data, and interrogation transcripts compiled after the 1878 uprising [4]."}]
22:["$","p","p-6",{"children":"Agnes grew up on St. Croix, living and working within the network of sugar plantations that dominated the island’s economy. She was a member of the Moravian Church, a Protestant denomination that had a significant presence in the Danish West Indies and provided one of the few avenues of education and spiritual community for the Black population [4]."}]
23:["$","p","p-7",{"children":"By the time of the rebellion in 1878, Agnes was an unmarried young woman of about twenty. She was already a mother of three children, a testament to the immense domestic and financial responsibilities she carried while laboring in the sugarcane fields [4]. Her daily life was defined by the double burden of agricultural labor under the hot Caribbean sun and the care of her young family, all within the constraints of the restrictive 1849 Labor Act."}]
24:["$","h3","h3-3",{"children":"The Spark: October 1, 1878 (Contract Day)"}]
25:["$","p","p-8",{"children":"On October 1, 1878, thousands of plantation workers from across St. Croix traveled to the port town of Frederiksted, which served as the commercial center for the island’s sugar trade. It was Contract Day, and the town was filled with laborers seeking to renew their agreements, change employers, or celebrate the brief moment of mobility granted by the law [2]."}]
26:["$","p","p-9",{"children":"Tensions were high. Workers had hoped that the colonial government would announce the repeal of the Labor Act and a raise in the daily wage. When it became clear that no reforms were forthcoming, peaceful protests turned into angry demonstrations [3]. The situation escalated dramatically when a rumor spread through the crowd that a popular laborer named Henry Plum had been severely beaten by colonial police and had died in the local hospital."}]
27:["$","p","p-10",{"children":"Enraged by this apparent act of police brutality, the crowd descended upon the Frederiksted Fort (Fort Frederik), where the local police and military had barricaded themselves [2]. Lacking firearms, the workers used stones, sticks, and tools to attack the fort. When the military fired into the crowd, killing several protesters, the demonstration erupted into a full-scale insurrection [3]. The laborers, realizing they could not breach the fort’s stone walls, turned their anger toward the town itself, systematically setting fire to the commercial buildings and sugar warehouses."}]
28:["$","h3","h3-4",{"children":"The Carlton Plantation Uprising and Agnes's Leadership"}]
29:["$","p","p-11",{"children":"As the fires consumed Frederiksted, the rebellion spread outward into the rural plantation districts [2]. The workers organized themselves into groups, marching from estate to estate, dismantling machinery, and burning sugarcane fields and plantation houses. It was during this phase that Axeline Salomon emerged as a key strategist and leader, earning the title \"Queen.\""}]
2a:["$","p","p-12",{"children":"On the morning of Wednesday, October 2, 1878, Agnes was active at the Carlton Plantation, a large sugar estate located east of Frederiksted [5]. Carlton became the site of a violent clash. A group of Danish soldiers, sent to reinforce Frederiksted, had left a military cart at the plantation. A crowd of rebels, including Agnes, confronted the soldiers. In the ensuing struggle, two Danish soldiers were killed [5]."}]
2b:["$","p","p-13",{"children":"According to later testimonies from witnesses and co-defendants, Agnes played an active role in inciting the violence at Carlton [4]. She was described as carrying a lantern, using its flame to ignite the dry trash in the sugarcane fields and urging the crowd to confront the military. Interrogation records from the Commission of 1878 detail how Agnes spoke openly about the events, displaying a bold lack of fear that inspired her peers [4]."}]
2c:["$","p","p-14",{"children":"The rebellion raged for several days, destroying over fifty plantations and causing massive economic damage to the Danish colony [2]. The colonial governor deployed the military, supported by armed volunteers and sailors from foreign warships, to ruthlessly suppress the uprising. Over a hundred Black laborers were shot or executed, and hundreds more were arrested."}]
2d:["$","h3","h3-5",{"children":"The Colonial Crackdown and Trial"}]
2e:["$","p","p-15",{"children":"In the wake of the Fireburn, Danish authorities established a special military commission to investigate the rebellion and punish the leaders. Axeline Salomon was arrested and subjected to intense interrogation [4]. The trial records, preserved in the Danish National Archives, reveal the bias of the colonial judicial system, which was designed to protect the interests of the plantocracy and assert colonial dominance."}]
2f:["$","p","p-16",{"children":["Despite these hostile conditions, Agnes and her co-defendants, including ",["$","$L1d","a-0",{"slug":"queen-mary","href":"/profiles/queen-mary","children":"Queen Mary"}]," and ",["$","$L1d","a-1",{"slug":"queen-mathilda","href":"/profiles/queen-mathilda","children":"Queen Mathilda"}],", remained defiant. On September 2, 1880, the commission sentenced Axeline Salomon to death for her role in the rebellion, specifically for her participation in the Carlton Plantation killings and arson [4]. The Supreme Court in Copenhagen confirmed the death sentence on May 23, 1881 [4]."]}]
30:["$","p","p-17",{"children":"However, executing three women who had become folk heroines threatened to spark further unrest. Seeking to defuse the situation, King Christian IX of Denmark commuted the death sentences of Agnes, Mary, and Mathilda to life imprisonment at hard labor [4]."}]
31:["$","h3","h3-6",{"children":"Exile and Imprisonment in Copenhagen"}]
32:["$","p","p-18",{"children":["In July 1882, Agnes, Mary Thomas, and Mathilda McBean were placed aboard the Danish naval ship ",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"Valdemar"}]," and transported across the Atlantic to Denmark [2]. They were incarcerated in the Kvindefængslet på Christianshavn (the women's prison in Christianshavn, Copenhagen) [4]."]}]
33:["$","p","p-19",{"children":"The transition from the tropical climate of St. Croix to the cold, damp cells of Copenhagen was brutal. The women faced severe culture shock, freezing winters, and isolation. In prison, they were forced to perform hard labor, primarily sewing, knitting, and cleaning. Agnes’s prison records note that she arrived with almost no personal belongings, carrying only a single pair of earrings [4]."}]
34:["$","p","p-20",{"children":["Despite their imprisonment, the \"Queens of the Fireburn\" captured the imagination of the Danish public. They were visited by journalists and artists, who were struck by their dignity and resilience. Their legacy of resistance was similar in spirit to other Caribbean slave rebellions, such as those led by ",["$","$L1d","a-0",{"slug":"bussa","href":"/profiles/bussa","children":"Bussa"}]," in Barbados, ",["$","$L1d","a-1",{"slug":"sam-sharpe","href":"/profiles/sam-sharpe","children":"Sam Sharpe"}]," in Jamaica, and ",["$","$L1d","a-2",{"slug":"tula","href":"/profiles/tula","children":"Tula"}]," in Curaçao, showing a shared regional history of fighting against colonial bondage."]}]
35:["$","h3","h3-7",{"children":"Return to St. Croix"}]
36:["$","p","p-21",{"children":"After serving several years in Denmark, the colonial administration decided to return the women to St. Croix. The cost of maintaining them in Copenhagen, combined with concerns about their health and growing public sympathy in Denmark, prompted their repatriation. In the late 1880s, Agnes, Mary, and Mathilda were sent back to St. Croix, where they were incarcerated at the Bassin Jailhouse in Christiansted to serve out the remainder of their sentences [2]."}]
37:["$","p","p-22",{"children":"The traditional folk song of St. Croix commemorates their return and the memory of the jailhouse:"}]
38:["$","blockquote","blockquote-0",{"children":["\n",["$","p","p-0",{"children":[["$","em","em-0",{"children":"Queen Mary, oh where you gon' go burn?"}],"\n",["$","em","em-1",{"children":"Queen Mary, oh where you gon' go burn?"}],"\n",["$","em","em-2",{"children":"Don't ask me nothin' at all."}],"\n",["$","em","em-3",{"children":"Just give me the match and oil."}],"\n",["$","em","em-4",{"children":"Bassin Jailhouse, ah there the money there."}]," [1]"]}],"\n"]}]
39:["$","p","p-23",{"children":"Agnes was eventually released from prison, though the exact date of her release and her life afterward remain obscured by history. She lived out her final years on the island she had fought to liberate, witnessing the gradual decline of the Danish colonial system."}]
3a:["$","h3","h3-8",{"children":"Legacy and Commemoration"}]
3b:["$","p","p-24",{"children":["Axeline \"Queen Agnes\" Salomon’s legacy is celebrated throughout the Virgin Islands. She represents the intersection of racial, class, and gender resistance in Caribbean history. In a society that sought to render Black working-class women invisible, Agnes forced her way into the historical record through her courage and leadership. Her struggle for labor rights echoed across the region, matching the later efforts of figures like ",["$","$L1d","a-0",{"slug":"clement-payne","href":"/profiles/clement-payne","children":"Clement Payne"}]," in Barbados and ",["$","$L1d","a-1",{"slug":"hamilton-jackson","href":"/profiles/hamilton-jackson","children":"David Hamilton Jackson"}]," in St. Croix."]}]
3c:["$","p","p-25",{"children":"To honor her and her fellow leaders, the \"Three Queens Fountain\" was erected at Blackbeard’s Castle in Charlotte Amalie, St. Thomas. The monument features bronze statues of Queen Mary, Queen Agnes, and Queen Mathilda. Agnes is depicted holding a lantern, a tribute to her role in lighting the fires of resistance that swept across St. Croix in 1878 [2]."}]
3d:["$","p","p-26",{"children":"Every year on October 1st, Virgin Islanders celebrate Contract Day, reciting the names of the Queens and singing the folk songs that preserve their memory. Queen Agnes remains an enduring symbol of the fight for labor rights, freedom, and human dignity in the Caribbean."}]
3e:["$","p","p-27",{"children":["$","img","img-0",{"src":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/5a/Frederiksted%2C_St_Croix_U.S._Virgin_Islands.JPG","alt":"Frederiksted, St. Croix, where the Fireburn rebellion began on October 1, 1878"}]}]
3f:["$","$L42",null,{"title":"Learn about the legacy of Queen Agnes","url":"https://caribbeanlegacyarchive.com/profiles/queen-agnes"}]
43:T4af,Axeline "Queen Agnes" Elizabeth Salomon was a key leader of the 1878 St. Croix labor rebellion, widely known as the "Fireburn," which challenged the oppressive post-emancipation labor laws in the Danish West Indies. Alongside other leaders like Queen Mary, Queen Agnes organized plantation workers to revolt against the restrictive 1849 Labor Act, which had bound formerly enslaved workers to sugar estates in a system of debt peonage and forced contracts. Her actions, particularly in mobilizing workers and organizing resistance at the Carlton Plantation, were central to the rebellion that ultimately forced the colonial administration to repeal the restrictive Labor Act in 1879, granting workers freedom of contract and mobility.

Today, Queen Agnes is commemorated as a national heroine of the U.S. Virgin Islands. She is memorialized in public monuments like the Three Queens Fountain in Charlotte Amalie, St. Thomas, where she is depicted holding a lantern—a symbol of the fire of resistance and the light of freedom. Her legacy is celebrated annually on Contract Day (October 1st) as an enduring symbol of working-class female leadership and anti-colonial resistance in Caribbean history.40:["$","div",null,{"className":"mb-12 pt-12 border-t border-gold/10","children":[["$","h2",null,{"className":"font-serif font-bold text-3xl text-navy mb-6","children":"Major Contributions"}],["$","div",null,{"className":"text-navy/80 text-xl leading-relaxed bg-white p-8 border-l-4 border-tropical-green shadow-sm","children":"$43"}]]}]
